subject: Biology
title: The Great Wildebeest Migration
description: A quick, practical guide to The Great Wildebeest Migration.

hook.text: Every year, 1.5 million wildebeest cross the Serengeti—the largest land migration on Earth.

buildup.text: They follow the rains in a clockwise loop through Tanzania and Kenya, chasing fresh grass.

discovery.text: Crocodiles wait at river crossings. Lions patrol the plains. Thousands die. The herd moves on.

twist.text: The migration fertilizes the ecosystem—wildebeest droppings deposit nutrients across the savanna.

climax.text: If fences or climate change block the route, the entire ecosystem collapses.

punchline.text: 1.5 million animals chasing rain across a continent.

quiz.question: How many wildebeest migrate across the Serengeti each year?

details.summary: Over 1.5 million wildebeest along with zebras and gazelles circle the Serengeti-Mara ecosystem annually, following rainfall and fresh grass. This migration shapes the entire savanna ecosystem through grazing, nutrient transport, and predator-prey interactions.
details.whyItMatters: The Great Migration is the largest mammal movement on Earth and a keystone ecological process. It demonstrates how animal behavior connects distant habitats and sustains biodiversity across vast landscapes.
takeaways: Over 1.5 million wildebeest migrate in a continuous annual circuit
Migration timing follows seasonal rainfall and grass growth patterns
River crossings involve massive predation by crocodiles and drowning

faq.question: What triggers the wildebeest to start migrating?
faq.answer: Rainfall and the resulting grass growth are the primary triggers. Wildebeest detect approaching rain through changes in atmospheric pressure and distant thunder, moving toward fresh grazing. The herd follows a roughly clockwise circuit through the year.

faq.question: How many animals die during the migration?
faq.answer: Approximately 250,000 wildebeest die annually from exhaustion, predation, drowning, and disease. However, around 500,000 calves are born each year during a synchronized calving season, sustaining the population despite heavy losses.
